title: Ya vs Todavía: Already, Still, Yet and No Longer in Spanish

body_html:
Ya vs todavía covers four English ideas: already, still, yet and no longer. Ya means something has happened or changed (already, now, no longer with no). Todavía means something continues or hasn’t happened (still, and yet with no). Put simply: Ya marks a change, todavía marks continuity. And aún is a common synonym of todavía.

Quick answer
  • Ya = already: Ya he comido.
  • Todavía / aún = still: Todavía vivo aquí.
  • Todavía no / aún no = not yet: Todavía no ha llegado.
  • Ya no = not anymore, no longer: Ya no fumo.
{{toc}}

Ya vs todavía: the core rule

EnglishSpanishExample
alreadyyaYa lo sé. I already know.
no longer, not anymoreya noYa no trabajo allí. I don’t work there anymore.
stilltodavía / aúnTodavía está dormido. He’s still asleep.
not yettodavía no / aún noAún no he terminado. I haven’t finished yet.
yet? (questions)ya¿Ya has comido? Have you eaten yet?

The RAE dictionary defines todavía as “until a given moment, from an earlier time”, and ya as referring to something past or completed.

Ya: change and completion

  • Ya he terminado. I’ve already finished.
  • ¿Ya te vas? Are you leaving already?
  • Ya es tarde. It’s late now.
  • Ya no vivo con mis padres. I don’t live with my parents anymore.

Note that questions with “yet” in English use ya in Spanish: ¿Ya llegó el paquete? (Has the package arrived yet?).

Todavía and aún: continuity

  • Todavía te quiero. I still love you.
  • Aún estamos esperando. We’re still waiting.
  • Todavía no sé qué hacer. I still don’t know what to do.
  • Todavía es pronto. It’s still early.

Careful: aún (with accent) means still; aun (without accent) means even: Aun así, voy (Even so, I’m going).

{{image:2}}

Todavía and comparisons

With comparatives, todavía and aún mean “even”: Hoy hace todavía más calor que ayer (It’s even hotter today than yesterday). Ya is never used this way.

The many meanings of ya

Ya is one of the most versatile words in spoken Spanish:

  • ¡Ya voy! I’m coming! (see {{link:ir-vs-venir|ir vs venir}})
  • Ya está. Done. / That’s it.
  • Ya veremos. We’ll see.
  • Ya, ya. Yeah, right. / I know, I know.
  • ¡Ya basta! That’s enough!
  • Ya que… Since… (because): Ya que estás aquí, ayúdame.
  • Desde ya: right away (Latin America).
{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Why this pair is tricky for learners

English “yet” behaves differently in questions and negatives: “Have you eaten yet?” and “I haven’t eaten yet”. Spanish uses different words for these: ¿Ya has comido? but Todavía no he comido. Learners also translate “not anymore” word by word and end up with no más, which in standard Spanish means “only” or “just” (though no más or nomás has other uses in Mexico and the Andes). The fix: learn ya no and todavía no as fixed two-word units.

A quick mental shortcut

Draw a timeline. If something has crossed a line (it happened, or it stopped), use ya. If it hasn’t crossed the line yet (it continues, or it hasn’t started), use todavía. Ya llegó: crossed. Todavía no llegó: not crossed. Ya no viene: stopped coming. Todavía viene: still comes.

Real conversation

  • A: ¿Ya has hablado con el casero? (Have you talked to the landlord yet?)
  • B: Todavía no. Ya no contesta mis mensajes. (Not yet. He doesn’t answer my messages anymore.)
  • A: ¿Y todavía quieres seguir en ese departamento? (And you still want to stay in that apartment?)
  • B: Ya veremos. (We’ll see.)

Regional notes

Both todavía and aún are used everywhere; todavía is slightly more frequent in conversation. In Mexico and parts of Central America you will hear ya mero (almost, nearly): Ya mero llego (I’m nearly there). In the Andes and Mexico, nomás adds softness or means “just”: Pásale nomás (Just come in). In Spain, ya on its own is a very common way of saying “I see” or “right” when listening: —Es que no tuve tiempo. —Ya. Depending on the tone, it can sound understanding or sceptical.

Remember too that ya can sit at the end of a sentence for emphasis: ¡Vámonos ya! (Let’s go now!).

Try it yourself

  1. I’ve already seen it. (Ya la he visto.)
  2. She’s still at work. (Todavía está en el trabajo.)
  3. They haven’t arrived yet. (Todavía no han llegado.)
  4. We don’t live there anymore. (Ya no vivimos allí.)
  5. Have you finished yet? (¿Ya has terminado?)

More pairs in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Ya marks a change: already, now, no longer. Todavía marks continuity: still, not yet. Learn ya no and todavía no as pairs, and enjoy the many everyday uses of ya.

faq.q: What is the difference between ya and todavía?
faq.a: Ya marks a change or completion (already, no longer with no). Todavía marks continuity (still, not yet with no).

faq.q: How do you say “not yet” in Spanish?
faq.a: Todavía no or aún no: Todavía no he terminado (I haven’t finished yet).

faq.q: How do you say “not anymore” in Spanish?
faq.a: Ya no: Ya no vivo aquí (I don’t live here anymore).

questions.q: Son las doce y ___ está durmiendo. (still)
___ no ha llamado. (He hasn’t called yet.)
___ no trabajo en esa empresa. (not anymore)
¿___ has comido? (Have you eaten yet?)
